sceneEn: A colleague is leaving and you are at their leaving party. Recall the time you spent together, say what they gave you, pass on your good wishes and get a promise to keep in touch.
partnerEn: a colleague who is moved and looking back
openingEn: Five years — I can hardly believe it. Do you remember how chaotic my first day was?
goalEn: A shared memory has been recalled, good wishes have been passed on and a concrete promise to keep in touch has been made.

sceneEn: A former teammate is asking you for a reference. Discuss which strengths you will write about, ask which example to use, say where the limit of your honesty lies and say when it will be ready.
partnerEn: an excited former teammate who wants a lot written about them
openingEn: Would that be all right with you? And could you write something about my leadership qualities too?
goalEn: Which strengths and which example will go in have been settled, the limit of honesty has been stated and a delivery time has been given.

sceneEn: You have gone back to your old home after a long time and you are talking to someone close: what has changed, how you have changed, where you feel you belong and how it will be from now on.
partnerEn: someone close who has missed you but has noticed you have changed
openingEn: You're back — and yet something is different. Is it us or is it you?
goalEn: What has changed has been described from both sides, the sense of belonging has been expressed and something has been said about what comes next.

sceneEn: You are discussing your preparation for C1 with a teacher: which skill you are good at, where you are weak, how long you need and how you will work.
partnerEn: a teacher who assesses honestly and likes making plans
openingEn: You've finished B2 — well done. Tell me honestly: where do you think there is still a gap?
goalEn: The strong and weak skills have been named, a timescale has been discussed and a concrete study plan has been settled.

sceneEn: You are having a review with your teacher at the end of B2: how the road has gone, what was hardest, what you can really do now, what you are proud of and what comes next.
partnerEn: an honest and supportive teacher who has followed you from the start
openingEn: A hundred lessons done. Before we close: what can you do today that you couldn't at the start?
goalEn: The road travelled, the hardest part and what you can now do have been described, and the next goal has been given.

sceneEn: You are in a board meeting and a hard decision has to be made. Say which options are in question, rule one out with reasons, state the scope of the decision and bring it to a resolution.
partnerEn: a board member who wants a quick decision and plays down the risks
openingEn: We've been going round in circles for two meetings. In your view, which options are still in question at all?
goalEn: The options in question have been listed, one has been ruled out with reasons, the scope of the decision has been stated and a resolution has been reached.

sceneEn: You are making a formal request to an institution: what you are applying for, which right you want to exercise, what reservation you have and when it takes effect. Use institutional language.
partnerEn: an official bound to the formalities who knows the set phrases by heart
openingEn: You'd like to submit an application — what exactly does your request relate to?
goalEn: The subject of the application, the right relied on and the date of effect have been made clear, and a reservation has been put on record.

sceneEn: You disagree with your superior's proposal in a meeting. First show that you have understood, put your objection in the subjunctive, justify your reservation and offer an alternative. If you are turned down, hold your position without damaging the relationship.
partnerEn: a senior manager attached to their proposal who takes objections personally
openingEn: I get the impression you're not convinced. Do say it straight out — what's bothering you?
goalEn: The objection has been made with reasons and tact, an alternative has been offered and the conversation has been brought to a conclusion without damaging the relationship.

sceneEn: A colleague has criticised you indirectly. Say what you have sensed, ask directly, put your own reservation without hiding it and clear the matter up between you.
partnerEn: a colleague who avoids speaking plainly and talks in hints
openingEn: Well, in itself your draft is fine. Actually I'd only have … well, done it differently. Do you know what I mean?
goalEn: The criticism behind the hint has been said openly, both sides have put their reservations directly and the matter has been cleared up.

sceneEn: Something has gone wrong at your organisation and a journalist is talking to you. Express regret, describe what happened in corporate language, say which measures have been started and say when you will report back.
partnerEn: an insistent journalist looking for someone to blame and wanting a name
openingEn: Who bears the responsibility for this? And please don't tell me that measures have been initiated.
goalEn: Regret has been expressed, the incident and the measures have been described, the question of responsibility has been met rather than dodged and a date for the next update has been given.

sceneEn: You are putting a new subject on the table in a negotiation that has long been stuck. Open the subject, say what risk you are taking on, say what you want in return and bring it to a conclusion or a further round.
partnerEn: an experienced and patient counterpart who does not concede easily
openingEn: We're at the same point as three weeks ago. Have you brought anything new?
goalEn: A new subject has been put on the table, the risk taken on and the return asked for have been stated and it has been brought to a conclusion or a further round.

sceneEn: You are running a project without any formal authority and someone on the team is letting their work slip. Name the problem, give direction without giving orders, leave the responsibility with them and say you will support them.
partnerEn: a well-meaning team member who questions your authority
openingEn: With respect — you're not formally my line manager. Why should I do it that way now?
goalEn: The problem has been named, direction has been given without an order, the responsibility has been left with them and support has been promised.

sceneEn: You are talking to a colleague after a meeting: work out together what the jargon in the meeting actually meant, make clear who has taken on what and settle the next step.
partnerEn: a colleague fluent in the jargon but open to making things clear
openingEn: 'We'll take that away and align on it afterwards' — honestly, do you know who's doing what now?
goalEn: The real meaning behind the jargon has been worked out, who has taken on what has been made clear and the next step has been tied to a date.

sceneEn: You are giving a three-minute pitch to an investor. Bring the listener in, state the problem and the solution, explain what sets you apart, answer the 'why now' question and ask for a next step.
partnerEn: an investor who cuts you short and asks hard questions
openingEn: You have three minutes. And please don't start with the company history — what problem are you solving, and with what?
goalEn: The problem, the solution and what sets you apart have been described, 'why now' has been answered and a concrete next step has been asked for.

sceneEn: You are mediating between two colleagues. Report what each side has said impartially, find the common ground, make a suggestion and bring them to a step both will accept.
partnerEn: a colleague certain they are in the right and unwilling to hear the other side
openingEn: Let me say straight away: I have done nothing wrong. What has the other side claimed, then?
goalEn: Both sides' views have been reported impartially, common ground has been found and a step both accept has been agreed.

sceneEn: A friend does not want to come to an event. Invite them, argue against their reasons, answer their negative questions with the positive 'doch' and bring it to a decision.
partnerEn: a reluctant friend who finds an excuse for everything but can be talked round
openingEn: You're not seriously trying to talk me into this thing, are you?
goalEn: The invitation has been made, the excuses have been argued against and it has been decided whether your friend is coming.

sceneEn: You have run into someone in the street you have not seen for a long time. Show your surprise, ask them to tell you something, give your own news and arrange something to meet again.
partnerEn: an old acquaintance who is delighted to see you and has a lot to tell
openingEn: I don't believe it — is that really you? How long has it been now?
goalEn: News has been exchanged both ways and something concrete has been arranged to meet again.

sceneEn: Something has gone wrong that you cannot change (a cancellation, a delay, a missed chance). Talk to a friend: say what happened, say you are angry, then move into the tone of acceptance and settle what you will do next.
partnerEn: a friend who tries to fix it first and then accepts it with you
openingEn: And there's really nothing more to be done? Nothing at all?
goalEn: The setback has been described, the anger has been voiced, the tone has moved to acceptance and a step for what comes next has been settled.

sceneEn: You and a colleague are talking about a decision that has not been announced. Give your guesses while showing you are not sure, keep apart what you have grounds for and what you have not, and decide what you will do.
partnerEn: a colleague who likes to speak in certainties and presents guesses as facts
openingEn: They'll have decided it long ago. Or have you got any grounds to think otherwise?
goalEn: What is grounded and what is not have been separated, the guesses have been given without certainty and it has been settled what to do.

sceneEn: A friend has had bad news and is low. Listen first, then calm them, give hope without overdoing it and offer something concrete.
partnerEn: a sad friend who is not easily comforted but wants to talk
openingEn: Please don't tell me it'll all be fine again. I've heard that so often — what is there to get better?
goalEn: Your friend has been heard, calmed without empty comfort, and concrete help has been offered.

sceneEn: You are waiting on a piece of work and the other side keeps putting it off. Show your impatience in measure, give a warning, acknowledge that you are pressing them and agree a deadline.
partnerEn: someone who keeps putting it off and always has an excuse ready
openingEn: I know, I know — I'm on it. Does it really have to be today?
goalEn: Impatience has been shown in measure, a warning has been given and a binding deadline has been agreed.

sceneEn: You are giving your verdict on a colleague's work. Give measured praise, say what is lacking politely, explain if they ask whether you disliked it, and give a clear conclusion.
partnerEn: a colleague used to lavish praise who finds measured language cold
openingEn: 'Not bad' — does that mean good or bad? One never knows with you lot.
goalEn: Measured praise and polite criticism have been given separately, the misunderstanding has been cleared up and a clear conclusion has been stated.

sceneEn: You are making small talk with a stranger at a work function. Open the conversation, find a subject in common, take it further with an impersonal question and leave politely.
partnerEn: a polite guest who is quiet at first and opens up as they talk
openingEn: Hardly anyone knows anyone here, do they? Do you come to these things often?
goalEn: The conversation has been opened, a subject in common has been found and the talk has been closed with a polite goodbye.

sceneEn: You are ringing an institution and the person you need is not there. Explain your situation politely, ask to be put through, leave a message if that fails and arrange a time for a call back.
partnerEn: a switchboard operator who sticks to the rules and does not put people through easily
openingEn: Good afternoon, switchboard. I'm afraid Mr Baumann is not in the building today — what is it about?
goalEn: The matter has been explained, a message has been left and a time for a call back has been arranged.

sceneEn: You are talking to a friend about something that has upset your plans. Change your tone three times in the conversation: first inviting and softening, then mild reproach, and at the end comfort and acceptance.
partnerEn: a friend who upset the plan, defensive at first but apologising in the end
openingEn: Tell me, are you cross now? It really wasn't my fault.
goalEn: The reproach has been voiced, the other side's reasons have been heard and the conversation has closed with acceptance and a new plan.
